summary: Sol Watch is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12 that turns real NASA data into one simple choice. The child creates their own astronaut and commands a small base on Mars. A real solar storm is coming, taken from NASA's DONKI record of solar flares since 2010. The child shares 10 power cubes between three jobs: air and warmth, a storm shelter, and science. More power for one job always means less for the others. If the shelter is too weak, the radiation badge passes NASA's 250 mSv limit and the game is over. If life support is too low, the base freezes. After every mission, the game explains in plain words what happened, why, what it cost and what to try next, with a real astronaut fact. Sol Watch runs on laptops and phones, in English and Bahasa Melayu, with no login. A Class mode lets whole classrooms compete as teams against the same real storm. Our goal: children learn how real missions are planned, because every choice costs something.

3.1 What does it do, and how does it work?

Sol Watch is a mission trainer game. Each mission is one day on Mars (24 game hours, about 3 minutes of play) against one real solar flare recorded by NASA. The player is the commander, and the real Sun is the opponent. 

Step 1: Make Your Astronaut

The child picks a suit, visor, helmet extra, mission patch and name, then their birthday. Their astronaut then stands inside the 3D base for the whole mission.

Figure 1. The astronaut creator. The same astronaut appears inside the 3D Mars base.

 

Step 2: Home Page

Today's Sun shows the newest real flare from NASA, with a 3D Sun the child can turn. From here the child starts today's mission, plays their birthday storm, opens the Storm Time Machine (any day since 2010), or tries the other missions.

Figure 2. The home page: today's real solar storm from NASA, the birthday storm and the Storm Time Machine.

 

Step 3: Plan

Bolt, a friendly robot, reads a 4-picture guide aloud before the first mission. The child sends the rover out for science but must bring it home before the storm, then guesses whether the battery will last the night. Then comes the main choice: sharing 10 power cubes between Air and warmth, Storm shelter and Science. Under each job, a plain-words hint says what will happen, for example “Too little! The crew will get cold.”

Figure 3. Sharing 10 power cubes. Each job explains what that many cubes will do.

 

Step 4: Play From Inside The Base

The camera stays over the astronaut's shoulder. In daylight the solar panels charge the battery, and at night the battery drains. A warning travels from Earth to Mars, and Bolt warns when the crew gets cold or radiation rises. When the real storm arrives, the child can move their cubes once, and a blue shield bubble shows how well the shelter protects them.

Figure 4. Playing from inside the base, with meters showing faces and the NASA radiation limit line.

 

Step 5: Bolt's Quick Question.

Once per mission, in a calm moment, the clock pauses for a space question with picture answers. The answer is always explained, and a right answer earns a brain star.

Figure 5. Bolt's quick question, answered and explained.

 

Step 6: Game Over Or Stars.

If the radiation badge passes NASA's 250 mSv limit, or the base gets too cold, the astronaut is knocked down and a GAME OVER card names the exact cause and what to try next. Otherwise the child earns 1 to 3 stars. Result cards explain What happened, Why, What it cost and Next time, built from the child's actual plan. They also show a real astronaut fact with its NASA source, and Rewind lets the child compare another plan.

Figure 6. Game over: the real reason (here, the rover trip was too long) and the dose against NASA's limit.

Figure 7. A win: every card is written from what really happened in this mission.

 

Class mode

 A teacher runs a team battle on one screen in 7 steps:

1.     Pick 2 to 4 teams and one real NASA storm (medium, strong or giant).

2.     Meet the crew and use the 60-second team talk timer.

3.     Each team places its 10 power cubes.

4.     Each team predicts its stars.

5.     All missions race side by side.

6.     A podium explains each result.

7.     A 5-question quiz round, followed by the final scoreboard.

Figure 8. Class mode: every team's mission races against the same real storm.

Figure 9. Class mode podium: each team's result explained.

 

How it works inside?

The game logic is a set of pure, deterministic TypeScript functions, so the same plan and storm always give the same result. A build script turns NASA's DONKI records into an archive of 2,776 M- and X-class flares. For each flare, its class sets the storm strength, the gap until its particle event sets the warning time, and the linked geomagnetic storm gives the Earth impact. A Vercel serverless function fetches today's storm live, and falls back to the archive if NASA cannot be reached.

3.2 What benefits does it have?

Learning by deciding: children make the trade-off themselves and see the result, instead of reading about it.

Real science, not made up: real NASA storms and real NASA radiation limits. Every number has a source.

Explains every result: in a child's words, from their own plan, with a tip for next time.

Free and private: no login, no ads, and no personal data collected. Progress stays on the device.

Works anywhere: laptops and phones. With 3D off, it shows real NASA photos instead.

Two languages: English and Bahasa Melayu, including Bolt's voice.

Ready for school: Class mode turns it into a 20-minute lesson, with teacher notes.

 

3.3 What is the intended impact?

Children understand that real space missions are about trade-offs, and learn four science ideas through play:

·       Radiation comes from the Sun.

·       Thick walls and water block radiation.

·       Solar panels only work in daylight.

·       Messages to Mars take minutes, so crews must decide for themselves.

Malaysian teachers get a free STEM lesson in Bahasa Melayu that uses real NASA data. We hope Sol Watch makes children curious about space careers, and shows them that open NASA data is something they can use themselves.

  

3.4 What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Languages - TypeScript, HTML, CSS, JSON
  • Frameworks and libraries - React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber (3D), Vitest (automated tests)
  • Browser features - Web Speech API (Bolt's voice), WebGL (3D), local storage (saves progress on the device)
  • Hosting and data - Vercel (website and serverless functions), GitHub (code), NASA Open APIs (DONKI)
  • AI coding tools - Kiro (AWS) and Claude (Anthropic). See section 4.
  • Hardware - Team laptops for building, and laptops and phones (Android and iPhone) for testing

3.5 How is our project creative?

The real Sun is the opponent. Every storm really happened, and children can play the storm from their own birthday.

The whole challenge in one simple choice. 10 power cubes and 3 jobs hold the trade-off between life support, shielding and science.

You play from inside the base. Your own astronaut stands at the command post, and gets knocked down if the storm gets through.

Every result is explained. Explanations are built from the child's own plan, not a fixed message.

A classroom race. Teams predict their stars, then watch their missions race against the same real storm.

3.6 What factors did our team consider?

  • Age 7 to 12 - Short sentences, picture guide, read-aloud, faces on meters, plain-word hints. Game over says “knocked out” and “rescued”, never anything frightening.
  • Scientific accuracy - Real NASA numbers with sources in the code. Anything not from NASA is labelled “game estimate”, both in the code and on the in-game NASA data page.
  • Fairness - 10 automated tests: no single job wins everything, a sensible plan can win every storm, and different plans always get different explanations.
  • Access and devices - Works on phones and older laptops (3D can be turned off). Keyboard controls, and meaning is never shown by colour alone.
  • Language - English and Bahasa Melayu, switchable at any time, for Malaysian schools.
  • Privacy - No accounts and no tracking. The birthday and progress are saved only on the device.
  • Reliability - If NASA's live data cannot be reached, the game uses the saved NASA archive and says so.
  • Classrooms - Class mode for one shared screen, with a timer, team turns, a quiz and teacher notes.
